title: Lagash-Umma dispute in ancient Sumeria over water and irrigation leads to a century of conflict
description: The dispute over water and irrigated lands in the Gu'edena (the "edge of paradise") region, between the Sumerian city-states of Umma and Lagash, lasts for a century in the first known water conflict.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Tigris River dammed in ancient dispute in Babylon
description: A grandson of Hammurabi, Abish or Abi-Eshuh, dams the Tigris to prevent the retreat of rebels led by Iluma-Ilum, who declares the independence of Babylon. This failed attempt marks the decline of the Sumerians who had reached their apex under Hammurabi.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Kishon River floods and contributes to the defeat of Sisera in the biblical battle between the Israelites and the Canaanites
description: The Old Testament gives an account of the defeat of Sisera and his "nine hundred chariots of iron' by the unmounted army of Barak on the fabled Plains of Esdraelon in the Battle of Mount Tabor between the Israelites and the Canaanites. In this account, God sends heavy rainfall in the mountains, and the Kishon River overflows the plain and immobilizes or destroys Sisera's forces ("...the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, and the clouds also dropped water," Judges 5:4; "...The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon,' Judges 5:21).
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Scofield 1967

title: Assyrian king Sargon II uses water as a weapon and target during multiple campaigns
description: In several military campaigns, King Sargon II of Assyria and his opponents both use water as a weapon and a target, damaging wells, diverting and destroying irrigation canals, and flooding lands for offensive and defensive purposes.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994 ; Melville 2016

title: Sennacherib razes Babylon and diverts an irrigation canal to wash over the ruins
description: In quelling rebellious Assyrians in 695 BCE, Sennacherib razes Babylon and diverts one of the principal irrigation canals so that its waters wash over the ruins.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Hezekiah stops springs in advance of Assyrian invasion led by Sennacherib
description: When King Hezekiah of Judah sees that Sennacherib of Assyria is coming in war, he has springs and a brook outside Jerusalem stopped to keep water from the Assyrians. ("So there was gathered much people together, who stopped all the fountains, and the brook that ran through the midst of the land, saying, Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water" 2 Chronicles 32:1"4).
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Scofield 1967

title: Assyrian king cuts off water of enemy in siege of Tyre
description: Esarhaddon, an Assyrian, refers to an earlier period when gods, angered by insolent mortals, created destructive floods. According to inscriptions recorded during his reign, Esarhaddon besieges Tyre, cutting off food and water.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Assyrian king dries up enemy's wells in a war against Elam
description: Ashurbanipal's inscriptions also refer to a siege against Tyre, although scholars attribute it to Esarhaddon. In campaigns against both Arabia and Elam in 645 BCE, Ashurbanipal, son of Esarhaddon, dries up wells to deprive Elamite troops. He also guards wells from Arabian fugitives in an earlier Arabian war. On his return from victorious battle against Elam, Ashurbanipal floods the city of Sapibel, and ally of Elam. According to inscriptions, he dams the Ulai River with the bodies of dead Elamite soldiers and deprives dead Elamite kings of their food and water offerings.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Khosr River diverted by Babylonians to cause a flood to support an attack on Nineveh
description: A coalition of Egyptian, Median (Persian), and Babylonian forces attacks and destroys Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. Nebuchadnezzar's father, Nabopolassar, leads the Babylonians. The converging armies divert the Khosr River to create a flood, which allows them to elevate their siege engines on rafts.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Nebuchadnezzar uses Euphrates River as defense of Babylon
description: Nebuchadnezzar builds immense walls around Babylon, using the Euphrates and canals as defensive moats surrounding the inner castle.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994 ; Drower 1954

title: Hellebore is used to poison water supplies during the Cirraean War, at the beginning of the 6th century BCE
description: Athenian legislator Solon reportedly has roots of Helleborus thrown into a small river or aqueduct leading from the Pleistrus River to Cirrha during a siege of this city. The enemy forces become violently ill and are defeated as a result. Some accounts have Solon building a dam across the Plesitus River cutting off the city's water supply. Such practices are widespread.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Absolute Astronomy n.d. ; Hippocrates 1990

title: Forces under Nebuchadnezzar breach an aqueduct to end siege of the ancient city of Tyre
description: Nebuchadnezzar breaches the aqueduct that supplies the city of Tyre in order to end a long siege.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Lorenz and Shaver 2003

title: Cyrus diverts the Diyalah River during his war against Nabonidus in Babylon
description: On his way from Sardis to defeat Nabonidus at Babylon, Cyrus faces a powerful tributary of the Tigris, probably the Diyalah. According to Herodotus' account, the river drowns his royal white horse and presents a formidable obstacle to his march. Cyrus, angered by the "insolence" of the river, halts his army and orders them to cut 360 canals to divert the river's flow. Other historians argue that Cyrus needed the water to maintain his troops on their southward journey, while another asserts that the construction was an attempt to win the confidence of the locals.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Cyrus diverts the Euphrates in his attack on Babylon
description: According to Herodotus, Cyrus invades Babylon by diverting the Euphrates above the city and marching troops along the dry riverbed. This popular account describes a midnight attack that coincided with a Babylonian feast.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: The city of Jinyang is flooded by the army of Zhi Yao in central China
description: In 454 BCE, during a conflict between the Jin and Zhao clans in central China, Zhi Yao of Jin builds a dam to divert the Fen River to inundate the city of Jinyang (now Taiyuan).
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Qian and Watson 1993

title: Spartans poison cisterns of Piraeus during the Peloponnesian War
description: During the second year of the Peloponnesian War, a plague breaks out in Athens. The Spartans are accused of poisoning the cisterns of the Piraeus, the source of most of Athens' water.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Tschanz 2006

title: Water is used as a weapon in the battle of Delium, 424 BC
description: In the battle of Delium, the Athenians are at war with the Theban Confederacy. It is a custom at that time not to damage sacred areas, such as the waters at the Delium temple. In this conflict, however, the Athenians foul the temple waters and destroy local vineyards and agricultural fields for a short-term military advantage.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hanson 1995 ; Finch 1996

title: Alexander tears down Persian dams and defensive weirs along the Tigris River
description: Returning from the razing of Persepolis, Alexander proceeds to India. After the Indian campaigns, he heads back to Babylon via the Persian Gulf and the Tigris, where he tears down defensive weirs that the Persians had constructed along the river. The Greek historian Arrian describes Alexander's disdain for the Persians' attempt to block navigation, which he saw as "unbecoming to men who are victorious in battle."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hatami and Gleick 1994

title: Alexander the Great conquers Cyropolis by infiltrating the city through a dried up waterway
description: Alexander the Great subdues the city of Cyropolis in 329 BC by laying siege to the city and sneaking through a dried-up watercourse that went under the town's wall, opening the city gates and admitting his invading army.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Arrian 1971

title: Chinese Qin general Bai Qi floods the city of Yicheng, reportedly drowning hundreds of thousands
description: In 278 BCE, Qin general Bai Qi attacks the capital of the state of Chu, flooding the city (now Yicheng) from the Yangtze River, and reportedly drowning hundreds of thousands of people.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Qian and Watson 1993

title: During the Chinese wars of unification an army redirects the waters of the Yellow River killing over 100,000 people
description: In 225 BC, a 600,000-strong Qin army led by Wang Ben during Qin's wars of unification laid seige to Daliang (present day Kaifeng, Henan, China). Wang Ben ordered his troops to redirect the waters from the Yellow River and the Hong Canal to flood Daliang and after three months of laboring, succeeded in their plan. Daliang was heavily flooded and over 100,000 people died, including civilians.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Bodde 1987

title: Parthian king Arsaces III destroys a water-supply system to slow the attacking army of Seleucid Antiochus
description: Around 210 BCE, Arsaces III, one of the Parthian kings, destroys qanats (underground channels) in order to make it difficult for the attacking army of Seleucid Antiochus to advance toward the Parthian capital, Hecatompylos.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Angelakis et al 2016

title: Thousands are drowned when Chinese general traps and then releases water during battles in 204 BCE
description: In 204 BCE, after the collapse of the Qin Dynasty and during extensive battles before the establishment of the Han Dynasty, Han general Han Xin lures an opposing Chu army into the Wei River and releases water held back by a dam, trapping and drowning thousands.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Qian and Watson 1993

title: Wei River dams in China are intentionally breached in 204 BC
description: An intentional rupturing of the Wei River dams leads to the victory of Han Dynasty forces.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Janku 2016

title: Water is used as a weapon in 101 BCE China in the siege of Fergana (Yuan)
description: Fergana (Yuan), the capital of China, surrenders after the enemy cuts off the city's water supplies. "In the city of the king of Yuan there were no wells, and the people had to obtain water from a river outside the city, whereupon experts in hydraulics were sent to divert the course of the river, thus depriving the city of water, besides effecting an opening though which the city might be laid open to access. General Ir-shi wished to attack Yu-chong but was afraid his detention might allow Yuan to resort to additional stratagems. He therefore went direct to Yuan, cut off the source of its water supply by diverting the course of the river upon which it depended, and the city was in great straits."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hirth 1917

title: Caesar constructs ditches as part of his blocade in the Siege of Alesia
description: Caesar constructs water-filled ditches as blockade during Siege of Alesia in Gaul, site of modern-day Alise-Sainte-Reine in Côte-d'Or near Dijon, France.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Caesar 52 BC

title: Caesar attacks water supplies during the siege of Uxellodunum
description: Caesar attacks water supplies during siege of Uxellodunum by undermining one of the local springs and placing attackers near the other. Shortage of water leads to the surrender of the Gauls.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; History of War Online n.d.

title: Massilia (modern-day Marseille) uses water to defend against Roman siege by Julius Caesar
description: During the first year of the Great Roman Civil War, Julius Caesar's troops lay siege to the walled city of Massilia (modern-day Marseille, France) using siege towers, battering rams, and by digging "mines" or tunnels to undermine the city walls. Massilians defend their city with "dogged determination;" tactics included directing water through pipes to wash down on attackers, which the Romans counter by covering siege buildings with bricks and "several coatings of stucco." Defenders also excavate a large basin inside the walls, filling it with water. As the Roman miners reach the walls, the tunnels are flooded with water and collapse. Massilia ultimately surrenders after a five-month siege.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Illustrated History of the Roman Empire n.d. ; Caesar 1906

title: Alexandria’s water supply disrupted during siege against Julius Caesar
description: In 48 BCE, Julius Caesar is besieged in Alexandria. General Ganimedes, chief of operations against Caesar, blocks the town’s water supply, causing panic in Caesar’s army. “By encouragement and reasoning Caesar allayed his men’s alarm, declaring that sweet water could be found in wells and trenches… whereupon a great quantity of sweet water was discovered.”
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Caesar et al 1955

title: Assyrians poison wells of enemies
description: Assyrians poison the wells of their enemies with rye ergot.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Eitzen and Takafuji 1997

title: The Achaeans use water as a weapon in the siege of Phana
description: Pausanias speaks of an Etolian town named Phana (perhaps the Paeanium of Polybius) besieged by the Achaeans, but without success. After an unsuccessful consultation with the Oracle of Delphi, the Achaeans accidentally discover the spring from which the besieged town derives its only supply of water. This being cut off, the town is forced to surrender.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Cramer 1828

title: Jewish protestors killed by Roman troops in protest over stream diversion
description: Roman Procurator Pontius Pilate uses sacred money to divert a stream to Jerusalem, Israel. The Jews are angered at the diversion and tens of thousands gather to protest. Pilate's soldiers mingle among the crowd and with daggers hidden in their garments, attack the protesters. "A great number" are slain and wounded.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Josephus 90 AD

title: The Chinese warlord Cao Cao floods the city of Xiapi at the end of the Han Dynasty in 199, forcing its surrender
description: In 199 AD at the end of the Han Dynasty, the warlord Cao Cao besieges the city of Xiapi (modern Pizhou) in eastern China, rerouting the rivers Yi and Si, and flooding the city, forcing its ultimate surrender.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Qian and Watson 1993

title: Goths cut aqueducts in their siege of Rome
description: In the 6th century AD, as the Roman Empire begins to decline, the Goths besiege Rome and cut almost all of the aqueducts leading into the city. In 537 AD this siege is successful. The only aqueduct that continues to function is the Aqua Virgo, which runs almost entirely underground.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Rome Guide 2004 ; InfoRoma 2004

title: To win a battle forces in Korea drown thousands of Chinese soldiers by building a dam and then releasing the water
description: The Goguryeo–Sui War launched by the Sui dynasty of China in the seventh century includes an attack by 300,000 troops against Pyongyang, the capital of Goguryeo. During the attack in 612, Goguryeo General Eulji Mundeok cuts off the flow of water in the Salsu river with a dam. When Sui troops reached the river, Mundeok opened the dam, flooding and killing thousands of enemy soldiers.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Ki-baik 1984 ; HistoryMaps 2024

title: The Tang Dynasty general Li Shimin builds and breaches a levee to flood the army of Liu Heit in China
description: In 622 AD, between the end of the Sui Dynasty and the start of the Tang Dynasty, the Tang general Li Shimin builds and then breaches a levee to defeat the rebel lord Liu Heit.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Qian and Watson 1993

title: The water Siege at the Battle of Karbala was a pivotal event in Islamic history, with the use of the Euphrates River as a weapon
description: In a pivotal event in Islamic history known as the Siege at the Battle of Karbala, water is used as a weapon by the Umayyad caliph Yazid's army against Imam Hussein bin Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad. During the siege, water from the Euphrates River is cut off from Hussein's forces.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Inloes 2024 ; Hussain 2005

title: The Chinese governor of Kaifeng in 1128 breaches dikes along the Yellow River in an effort to stop an advancing army
description: During the Chinese Jurchen “kingdom” (c. 1115 to 1234 AD) the governor of Kaifeng breaches the dikes along the Yellow River in a final, but futile effort to halt the advance of the Jurchen forces.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Chen et al. 2012 ; Storozum et al. 2018

title: In 1155 AD, in Tortona, Italy, Emperor Barbarossa poisons wells with human bodies
description: In 1155 AD, in Tortona, Italy, 12th-century Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa poisons wells with human bodies.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Rathish et al. 2025

title: Saladin cuts off Crusaders' water
description: Saladin is able to defeat the Crusaders at the Horns of Hattin in 1187 by denying them access to water. In some reports, Saladin fills all the wells along the way with sand and destroys the villages of the Maronite Christians who would supply the Christian army with water.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Lockwood 2001 ; Delli Priscoli 1998

title: Victims of a Viking conflict are tossed into a drinking water well and the water supply destroyed
description: In the year 1197, King Sverre Sigurdsson and Birkebeiner mercenaries are attacked and defeated by his rivals, the Baglers, in Sverresborg castle. A Viking legend tells that the Baglers destroy the buildings there as well as the freshwater supply of the castle, by disposing of victims in the well and filling it with stones. Recent archeological evidence confirms this legend.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Einem 2023

title: Mongols open dikes to flood the opposing Abbasid army as a prelude to attacking Baghdad
description: During the siege of Baghdad in 1258, Mongol forces break the levees of the Dujayl Canal and flood the camp of the opposing Abbasid army, drowning many and opening the way for the final attack on Baghdad.
basin: Mongol Empire and Abbasid Caliphate Havzası
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hua 2019 ; Boyle 1968

title: Water-supply canals and reservoirs are destroyed in Mughal, India in local protests over social and political conditions
description: Historian M. Athar Ali writes that in Mughal India, in the 1260s, the water canals and reservoirs feeding Delhi were intentionally dried up "because the channels feeding it were dammed up by 'dishonest men,'" referring to local protests over social and political conditions.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Sethi 2016

title: A flooding attempt by the Republic of Florence backfires
description: Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi develops a project to use the waters of the Serchio River to flood Lucca. During the attempt to change the course of the water, Lucca builds its own weir and instead of flooding the town, the water is diverted back into the fields flooding the Florentine camp.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Atkins 2008

title: Vlad the Impaler poisons wells in his battle with the Ottoman Empire in 1462
description: Prince Vlad III of Wallachia (Vlad the Impaler) poisoned wells in his battle with the Ottoman Empire and Sultan Mehmed II in 1462.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Rivero 2017

title: A siege during the Flemish revolt against Maximilian of Austria ends when a farmer diverts water from a moat
description: A siege against the Flemish succeeds when water in a moat is diverted away during the revolt by Flemish cities against Austrian rule.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Spijkers 2014

title: Machiavelli and Leonardo da Vinci develop a plan to cut Pisa's water
description: Leonardo da Vinci and Machiavelli plan to divert Arno River away from Pisa during conflict between Pisa and Florence (Italy).
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Honan 1996

title: Dutch flood land to repel Spaniards during the eighty years war, in what became known as the Dutch Water Line strategy
description: In 1573 at the beginning of the eighty years war against Spain, the Dutch flood the land to break the siege of Spanish troops on the town Alkmaar. The same defense is used to protect Leiden in 1574. This strategy becomes known as the Dutch Water Line and is used frequently for defense in later years.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Dutch Water Line 2002

title: Kenshin defeats Nobunaga forces in Japan by opening floodgates on the Tedori River
description: During the Battle of Tedorigawa in 1577 in Japan’s Kaga Province between the forces of Oda Nobunaga and Uesugi Kensin, Kensin orders floodgates on the Tedori River to be opened, killing Oda clan troops and repulsing their attack.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Acearchive 2023

title: Seawalls intentionally breached to relieve towns besieged by the Spanish during the Dutch war of independence against Spain
description: In order to relieve Antwerp, Campen, and Terneuzen during the Dutch war against the Spanish, seawalls are destroyed at Saeftinghe in February 1584, flooding more than 25,000 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: The Dutch flood more than 7,500 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the Eighty Years War with the Spanish Empire
description: The Dutch flood more than 7,500 hectares near Axel in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the Eighty Years War with the Spanish Empire.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: The Dutch flood more than 5,500 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during a conflict with the Portuguese
description: The Dutch flood more than 5,500 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during a conflict with the Portuguese.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: Spain attempts to re-route Rhine River to damage the Dutch economy
description: The Spanish Habsburgs attempt to prevent ship traffic on the River Rhine from reaching the Dutch Republic in order to damage the Dutch economy. Plans are also made to divert water from the Rhine to lands under Spanish control, to dry up downstream cities in Holland. The first stage is a canal between the Rhine and Meuse, between the cities of Rheinberg and Venlo. Plans for a later stage call for a connection between the Meuse and the Scheldt to circumvent the Scheldt Estuary, controlled by the Dutch. Although some 60 kms are constructed, the plan fails due to changed military conditions and lack of funding. Parts of the canal are still visible in present-day Germany.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Israel 1997 ; Bachiene 1791

title: 300,000 deaths when Yellow River dikes are breached in 1642
description: In 1642, in a battle between the incoming Manchu and the forces of the Ming dynasty, the Huang He River (Yellow River) dikes are breached by both sides, creating a catastrophe for Kaifeng in which 300,000 of its 378,000 citizens die.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hillel 1991 ; Janku 2016

title: Dutch flood land to repel French attack on the Netherlands
description: Louis XIV starts the third of the Dutch Wars in 1672, in which the French overrun the Netherlands. In defense, the Dutch open their dikes and flood the country, creating a watery barrier that is virtually impenetrable.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Columbia Encyclopedia 2000b

title: The Dutch flood around 3,500 hectares during a conflict with England, France, and two German electors
description: The Dutch flood around 3,500 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen and Flanders area during a conflict with England, France, and two German electors.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: The Dutch flood around 775 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the War of the Spanish Succession
description: The Dutch flood around 775 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the War of the Spanish Succession.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: The Dutch flood more than 2,200 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the War of Austrian Succession
description: The Dutch flood more than 2,200 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the War of Austrian Succession.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: Fire set in 1748 New York water dispute
description: Ferry house on Brooklyn shore of East River burns down. New Yorkers accuse Brooklynites of having set the fire as revenge for unfair East River water rights.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Museum of the City of New York (MCNY) n.d.

title: British attack the water system of New York during the Revolutionary War
description: British and Hessians attack the water-works system of New York: "...the enemy wantonly destroyed the New York water works' during the War for Independence."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Thatcher 1827

title: The Dutch flood around than 1,300 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the Anglo-Dutch wars
description: The Dutch flood around than 1,300 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during the Anglo-Dutch wars.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: The Dutch flood around than 9,500 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during a conflict with the French
description: The Dutch flood around than 9,500 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during a conflict with the French.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: Napoleon floods the plains around Mantua, Italy, to enhance the spread of malaria
description: Napoleon floods the plains around Mantua, Italy, to enhance the spread of malaria.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Riedel 2004

title: Wells polluted during the slave rebellion in Saint-Domingue, Hispaniola
description: A leader of the slave rebellion on the island of Hispaniola in the Caribbean, Toussaint L'Oueverture, says "The only resources we have are destruction and fire. Annihilate everything and burn everything. Block the roads, pollute the wells with corpses and dead horses."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hochschild 2006

title: Napoleon attempts to re-route Rhine River to harm Dutch
description: Napoleon orders the construction of a canal between Neuss and Venlo, to connect the Rhine and Meuse rivers, to divert trade from the Batavia Republic to the Southern Netherlands, then under French control. Three-quarters of the canal are completed, but work stops because of lack of funds.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Israel 1997

title: The French flood lands in the Netherlands to try to stop a British attack on Napolean's forces
description: During the effort of Britain to attack France's naval capacity in their fight against Napolean, they attempted to seize control of Walcheren and the port of Flushing in the Scheldt estuary in the Netherlands. The attack on Flushing was a success, though the French attempted to impeded the besiegers by cutting the dykes and flooding the land occupied by them. The flooding of the land led to a massive outbreak of malaria, typhus and typhoid fever and the British ultimately retreated.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hicks 2010

title: Russians destroy local water infrastructure to hinder the invasion by French Emperor Napoleon
description: Troops defending Russia against Napoleon’s invasion destroy or pollute existing water-supply infrastructure in order to deny its use by the French in 1812.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Willig and Hausler 2012

title: A reservoir destroyed in Canada over health fears
description: A reservoir in Ops Township, Upper Canada (now Ontario) is destroyed by neighbors who consider it a hazard to health.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Forkey 1998

title: A mob destroys reservoir in Ohio over health fears
description: A reservoir in Mercer County, Ohio is destroyed by a mob that considered it a health hazard.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Scheiber 1969

title: New Hampshire residents attack dam in dispute over water availability
description: Attack on a New Hampshire dam that impounds water for factories downstream by local residents unhappy over its effect on water levels.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Steinberg 1990

title: Mobs destroy canals in Indiana over health fears
description: Repeated destruction of the banks and reservoirs of the Wabash and Erie Canal in southern Indiana by mobs regarding it as a health hazard.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Fatout 1972 ; Fickle 1983

title: Water wells are poisoned during the US Civil War
description: General William T. Sherman's memoirs contain an account of Confederate soldiers poisoning ponds by dumping the carcasses of dead animals into them. Other accounts suggest this tactic was used by both sides.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Eitzen and Takafuji 1997

title: US Civil War Confederate forces use dams to cut off Union troops
description: During the US Civil War, Confederate forces near Yorktown use dams to flood the Warwick River and cut off Union troops. "The enemy is pushed behind a branch of the Warwick River in which they control the depths of water by dams. McClellan did not intend to pass that stream at that time, or at that point where the skirmish took place. But the troops, finding the stream fordable went over (under whose immediate orders does not appear) and the water was then deepened so that they were measurably cut off."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hitchcock 1862

title: Levees are cut by Union forces in Vicksburg, Virginia during the US Civil War
description: General Ulysses S. Grant, during the Civil War campaign against Vicksburg, cut levees in the battle against the Confederates.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Grant 1885 ; Barry 1997

title: Water violence in New Mexico over water rights
description: Recurrent friction and eventual violent conflict over water rights in the vicinity of Tularosa, New Mexico involving villagers, ranchers, and farmers.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Rasch 1968

title: Cattlemen fight Texan landowners for access to water and pasture
description: Drought in Texas in the early 1880s lead to growing disputes among ranch and land owners and cattlemen looking for access to grass and water for their stock. Cattlemen begin cutting fences to open access to water and pasture in what became known as the "Texas Fence Cutters Range War." At least three men are killed in clashes between fence cutters and ranchmen during this period, until agreements are reached.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Gard 2010 ; Carroll et al 1948

title: Mob dynamites Ohio reservoir
description: Dynamiting of a canal reservoir in Paulding County, Ohio by a mob regarding it as a health hazard. State Militia called out to restore order.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walters 1948

title: Canal lock destroyed in Canada
description: Partly successful attempt to destroy a lock on the Welland Canal in Ontario, Canada either by Fenians protesting English Policy in Ireland or by agents of Buffalo, NY grain handlers unhappy at the diversion of trade through the canal.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Styran and Taylor 2001

title: Many are killed during the Johnson County Water War between competing cattle association over access to water resources and land
description: The Johnson County Water War (or the War on Powder River) leads to many deaths among competing cattle interests. The conflict is fueled by pressure over water and land during severe droughts and hard winters in Wyoming and on the Great Plains.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Gleick 2023

title: France and Britain battle over control of the headwaters of the Nile River
description: Military conflict nearly ensues between Britain and France in 1898 when a French expedition attempts to gain control of the headwaters of the White Nile. While the parties ultimately negotiate a settlement of the dispute, the incident is since characterized as having "dramatized Egypt's vulnerable dependence on the Nile, and fixed the attitude of Egyptian policy-makers ever since."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Moorehead 1960

title: A deathly riot arises over the cost of water in Port of Spain, Trinidad
description: In 1903, the government in Port-of-Spain, Trinidad passes an ordinance increasing the price of water following the construction of national waterworks infrastructure. Public meetings are held to protest the increase, culminating in a riot at the seat of government, the Red House. Protestors set the building on fire and during the riot police kill 16 people and injure 42 others.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Mahoney 2013

title: German colonial troops poison desert water wells
description: German colonial troops brutally suppress a rebellion by the Herero people of German South-West Africa (modern-day Namibia). General Lothar von Trotha pledges to exterminate the Herero people in what has become known as the Herero and Namaqua Genocide. The Germans drive ethnic Herero and Namaqua populations into the Namib desert leading to massive death from dehydration and starvation; they also reportedly poison desert water wells. Later, the UN estimates that up to 100,000 were killed, or 70% of the Herero population.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Totten Parsons and Charny 2004 ; Kroll 2006

title: Five sticks of dynamite are found at the town well in Stratford, Iowa, USA but the bomb fails to explode
description: Five sticks of dynamite are found at the town well in Stratford, Iowa. The bomb fails to explode because of a faulty fuse.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Evening Times-Republican 1907

title: Violence over fishing and water access kills one in Tennessee
description: Violence, including a murder, directed against agents of a land company that claims title to Reelfoot Lake in northwestern Tennessee who attempt to levy charges for fish taken and threaten to drain the lake for agriculture.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Vanderwood 1969

title: Belgium floods land in an attempt to stop the German invasion in the First World War
description: During the early days of World War I in 1914 when the Germans invade Belgium, the French high command plan to flood land to obstruct the Germans. The plan is postponed because the Belgian army is preparing to flood the area between the Yser and its tributary canals, which happens in late October when the Belgians open the sluices at Nieuwpoort raising the water level until an impassable area is created due to flood water, forcing the Germans to retreat.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Edmonds 1925

title: Two powerful bombs are placed at the aqueduct that carries half of Glasgow, Scotland's water supply but they fail to go off
description: Two powerful bombs are placed at the aqueduct that carries half of Glasgow, Scotland's water supply but they fail to go off. A note stating the destruction of the aqueduct was a protest against the treatment of Emmeline Pankhurst, a leader of the British suffragette movement.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; San Bernardino County Sun 1914

title: German troops poison wells in Southwest Africa (now Namibia)
description: Union of South African troops capture Windhoek, capital of German Southwest Africa in May 1915. Retreating German troops poison wells - "a violation of the Hague convention."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Daniel 1995

title: During WWI, Germans devastate 30-km strip in 'Operation Alberich,' destroying water utilities to hinder Allied advance
description: Before the scheduled withdrawal of German forces in World War I from the Siegfried Line, the Germans devastate a 30-km-deep strip of land in ‘Operation Alberich’ to deprive advancing Allied troops of basic facilities, including water utilities and water infrastructure.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Willig and Hausler 2012

title: Two explosions destroy sections of the Los Angeles Aqueduct, California, USA
description: Two explosions destroy sections of the California aqueduct, in a protest against the diversion of water from the Owens Valley to Los Angeles.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Los Angeles Times 1917

title: Farmers bomb a canal to reduce diversions from a river in Idaho
description: Farmers angered by what they saw as excessive diversions from Mackay Reservoir on the Big Lost River in Idaho tried to blow up the dam. Reports say that when the farmers arrived at the dam wall, the operator said they didn’t have enough dynamite to do damage. He suggested targeting a specific diversion canal instead, and the explosion sent water back to the river’s natural channel.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Wittenberg 2019

title: Colorado River Compact Signed
description: Representatives of seven US Colorado River basin states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming) sign the Colorado River Compact in Santa Fe, dividing 15 million acre-feet of annual river flow equally between the Upper and Lower Basins, with Mexico excluded.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Colorado River Compact, Santa Fe (1922); US Bureau of Reclamation.

title: The concrete wall of the Alabama Gates of the Los Angeles Aqueduct is bombed, California, USA
description: The concrete wall of the Alabama Gates of the Los Angeles Aqueduct is bombed in protest of the taking of water from the Owens Valley, California.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: A city well feeding the Los Angeles Aqueduct, California, USA is bombed
description: A well feeding the Los Angeles Aqueduct to bring water from the Owens Valley to Los Angeles, California is bombed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: A ten-foot hole is blasted in Los Angeles Aqueduct, California, USA
description: A ten-foot hole is blasted in the Los Angeles Aqueduct near the Alabama Gates, in the ongoing violence protesting diversion of water from the Owens Valley to Los Angeles, California.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Yangtze River dikes in China are breached during battles between the National Revolutionary Army and a warlord
description: In 1926, the National Revolutionary Army of the Kuomintang (KMT) launches a military campaign to reunify China after the 1911 revolution. During battles, forces under the warlord Wu Peifu breach several Yangtze River dikes, temporarily slowing the advancing KMT army.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jordan 1976

title: A major section of the Los Angeles Aqueduct is destroyed by bombing, California, USA
description: A large section (the "No Name Siphon") of the Los Angeles Aqueduct is destroyed by bombing near Little Lake, California.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Bomb explodes in an attempt to block the Los Angeles Aqueduct with a landslide, California, USA
description: Bomb explodes in the Alabama Hills in an attempt to block the Los Angeles Aqueduct with a landslide.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Los Angeles Aqueduct and control gates are bombed in the Alabama Hills and separately, near Independence, California, USA
description: Two sections of aqueduct wall are damaged in separate bombings of the Los Angeles Aqueduct near the Alabama Hills and Independence, California. Control gates are also destroyed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Los Angeles Aqueduct is bombed again, near Tuttle Creek, Lone Pine, California, USA
description: The concrete wall of the Los Angeles Aqueduct at Tuttle Creek below Lone Pine, California is bombed, blowing a sixteen-foot hole in the aqueduct.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Los Angeles Aqueduct is bombed at Cottonwood Creek near Lone Pine, California, USA
description: The concrete wall of the Los Angeles Aqueduct at Cottonwood Creek below Lone Pine, California is bombed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: The water intake to a power plant in Big Pine, California, USA is bombed
description: The water intake to the city power plant in Big Pine, California is bombed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Anglo-Egyptian Nile Waters Agreement
description: Britain, representing Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika, and Sudan, signs an agreement with Egypt granting Egypt the right to veto upstream Nile projects and allocating 55.5 BCM annually to Egypt and 18.5 BCM to Sudan. Upstream African states are not consulted.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Exchange of Notes Between His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom and the Egyptian Government in regard to the use of the Waters of the River Nile for Irrigation Purposes, Cairo (1929).

title: A section of the Los Angeles Aqueduct is bombed in Kern County, California, USA
description: A ten-foot section of the Los Angeles Aqueduct is bombed in Kern County, California where the pipeline forms a siphon.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Walton 1992

title: Arizona mobilizes troops to protest Parker Dam and creates the "Arizona Navy."
description: Arizona calls out the National Guard and militia units to the border with California to protest the construction of Parker Dam and diversions from the Colorado River, briefly creating the "Arizona Navy"; the dispute ultimately is settled in court.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Reisner 1993

title: Dams are attacked during the Spanish Civil War
description: During the Spanish Civil War, two concrete gravity dams, at Burguillo and Ordunte, are attacked by the Nationalist army, with a 2.5-ton charge placed in an inspection gallery at Ordunte. Some limited damage occurs.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Pagan 2005

title: China destroys flood-control levees along the Yellow River to defend from Japan, with a very high death toll
description: Chiang Kai-shek orders the destruction of flood-control dikes of the Huayuankou, Henan section of the Huang He (Yellow) River, in order to flood areas threatened by the Japanese army. West of Kaifeng, dikes are destroyed with dynamite, spilling water across the flat plain. Even though the flood destroys part of the invading army and mires its equipment in mud, Wuhan, the headquarters of the Nationalist government is taken by the Japanese in October. Floodwaters cover an area variously estimated as between 3,000 and 50,000 square kilometers, and kill Chinese estimated in numbers between "tens of thousands" and "one million."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Hillel 1991 ; Lang 1994

title: 1939 Finns poison wells to combat invading Soviet troops
description: In the 1939-40 Russo-Finnish Winter War, Finns render wells unusable by putting animal carcasses or feces in them in order to combat invading Soviet forces.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Trotter 2000

title: Dutch flood valley to defend from Germany during World War II
description: During the mobilization of the Dutch at the beginning of World War II, 1939-40, the Dutch attempt to flood the Gelderse Vallei with the New Dutch Water Defense Line, which had been completed in 1885. During the German invasion in May 1940, large areas are inundated.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Information and Documentation Center for the Geography of the Netherlands (IDG) 1996

title: Japan's Unit 731 poisons wells in China
description: Japanese chemical and biological weapons activities reportedly include tests by 'Unit 731' against military and civilian targets in China by lacing water wells and reservoirs with typhoid and other pathogens.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Harris 1994

title: Finns use canal water against Soviets
description: Manipulation of the waters of the Saimaa Canal (Finland) by partisan Finns in order to flood surrounding land and hinder Soviet troop movements during the Soviet-Finnish conflict.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Malik 2005

title: Soviets create flood to slow German troops
description: In November 1941, Soviet troops flood the area to the south of the Istra Reservoir near Moscow in an effort to slow the German advance. Just a few weeks later, German troops use the same tactic to create a water barrier to halt advances by the Soviet 16th Army.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Malik 2005

title: The Dnipro Dam is targeted during World War II by both Soviets and Germans
description: The strategically-important Dnipro hydropower plant in Ukraine is targeted by both Soviet and German troops during WWII. On August 18, 1941, the dam and power plant are dynamited by Soviet troops retreating in front of advancing German forces. The facility is bombed again in 1943 by retreating German troops.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Pagan 2005 ; New York Times, The 1941 ; Makarov 2005 ; Axis History Forum 2004

title: The Soviet Union's hydroelectric dams are attacked during World War II
description: World War II inflicts enormous harm to hydroelectricity systems in the Soviet Union. Over two-thirds of the hydroelectric power stations are lost.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Malik 2005

title: The Dutch flood around than 5,800 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during World War II
description: The Dutch flood around than 5,800 hectares in the Zeeuws-Vlaanderen area during World War II.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: The water supply for Singapore is cut by the Japanese during the battle for Singapore in 1942
description: During the battle for Singapore in February 1942, the Japanese bombed the civilian water supply and cut off Singapore's water from Malaysia.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Baynes 2003

title: Ennepe Dam bombed in WWII
description: As part of the British "Dambusters" campaign in 1943 in World War II, the Ennepe Dam in the Ruhr Valley, Germany, is damaged.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Dar and Alam 2022

title: German dams on the Möhne, Sorpe, and Eder Rivers, Germany are destroyed by Allies
description: British Royal Air Force bomb dams on the Möhne, Sorpe, and Eder Rivers, Germany (May 16 and 17). Möhne Dam breech kills 1,200, destroys all downstream dams for 50 km. The flood that occurs after breaking the Eder dam reaches a peak discharge of 8,500 meters per second, which is nine times higher than the highest flood observed. Many houses and bridges are destroyed, and 68 are killed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Kirschner 1949 ; Semann 1950

title: Germans flood Ay River
description: Germans flood the Ay River in France in July 1944, creating a lake two meters deep and several kilometers wide, slowing an advance on Saint-Lô, a German communications center in Normandy.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; US Army Corps of Engineers 1953

title: Germans flood Ill River Valley
description: Germans flood the Ill River Valley during the Battle of the Bulge (winter 1944-45) creating a lake 16 kilometers long, 3-6 kilometers wide, and 1-2 meters deep, greatly delaying the American Army's advance toward the Rhine.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; US Army Corps of Engineers 1953

title: Germans flood land to hinder the invasion of Normandy
description: Germans flood land around Utah Beach and the area around the Douve River during the invasion of Normandy, France, in June 1944, hindering the advances of the US 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; War History Online 2016

title: Germans use Italian rivers against Allies
description: German forces use waters from the Isoletta Dam (Liri River, Italy) in January and February to successfully destroy British assault forces crossing the Garigliano River (downstream of Liri River). The German Army then dam the Rapido River, flooding a valley occupied by the American Army.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; US Army Corps of Engineers 1953

title: Germany floods Pontine Marshes
description: The German army floods the Pontine Marches, on the coast of Italy southeast of Rome, by stopping pumps and opening dikes, in order to disrupt Allied forces who had established a beachhead at Anzio, Italy. Allied forces are surrounded by German artillery and pinned down for months by heavy shelling. The purpose of the flooding is to bring mosquitoes and malaria, "deliberately introduced as an act of biological warfare." This has a limited military impact, but devastates the local population, which the Third Reich had wished to punish for disloyalty.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; US Army Corps of Engineers 1953 ; Evans 2009

title: October 1944: Allies breach dikes in Netherlands, flooding island and forcing German retreat; depicted in The Forgotten Battle
description: During the Battle of Walcheren Causeway in the Netherlands in October 1944, the Allies breach dikes protecting Walcheren Island, where German batteries blocked access to the port of Antwerp. These actions flood the central part of the island, forcing German defenders onto high ground. The Germans are ultimately forced to retreat. A film, The Forgotten Battle, commemorates these events.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Wikipedia

title: Soviets attack Finn-controlled dam near Leningrad
description: In June, the Soviet air force attacked the Svir River Dam near Leningrad, then under the control of the Finnish military.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Orlenko 1981 ; Axis History Forum 2004

title: The Nazis flood part of the Netherlands as a defense act during World War II
description: The Nazis flood more than 29,000 hectares in the islands of Schouwen-Duiveland and Tholen, St. Philipsland during World War II.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; de Kraker 2015

title: US targets Japanese water supplies in bombardment of Saipan
description: The US bombardment of the Japanese-occupied island of Saipan in June 1944 targets water-supply points, resulting in severe shortages.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Stewart n.d.

title: US-Mexico Treaty on Rio Grande and Colorado River
description: The United States and Mexico sign a landmark treaty governing the Rio Grande, Colorado, and Tijuana Rivers, allocating 1.5 million acre-feet of Colorado River water annually to Mexico and establishing water exchange obligations on the Rio Grande.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Treaty Between the United States of America and Mexico Relating to the Utilization of the Waters of the Colorado and Tijuana Rivers and of the Rio Grande (1944); IBWC.

title: During World War II Greek saboteurs attack water facilities, industries, and transportation systems
description: During World War II Greek saboteurs attack water facilities, industries, and transportation systems.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Douthit 1987

title: Germans pollute reservoir in Bohemia
description: In one of the few verified German tactical uses of biological warfare, German forces pollute a large reservoir in northwestern Bohemia, Czechoslovakia with sewage in May 1945. See also the entry for the Pontine Marshes in 1944.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) 1971

title: US bombing raid on Bangkok in World War II cuts off water and power to the city
description: A World War II B-29 raid on Bangkok destroys two key power plants leaving the city without power and water. This was the last major attack conducted against targets in Thailand prior to the Japanese surrender in August 1945.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Stearn 2003

title: In April 1948, India cuts the flow of Indus River irrigation water to Pakistan and the city of Lahore
description: In April 1948, India stops the flow of Indus River water to irrigation canals on its side, cutting off water to important agricultural areas in Pakistan and to the city of Lahore.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; McCaffrey 1993 ; Salman and Uprety 2002

title: Water and food supplies cut off during Arab siege of Jerusalem
description: Water and food supplies are cut off by Arab forces during their siege of Jerusalem from December 1, 1947 to July 10, 1948. Shortages cause Israelis to begin rationing water on May 12, limiting each person to 2 gallons per day (8 L), of which four pints (2 L) are for drinking.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Collins and LaPierre 1972 ; Joseph 1960 ; Wolf 1995 ; Wolf 1997

title: Zionist forces poison the water supply of the city of Acre and Gaza with infectious disease and bacteria
description: In May 1948, Zionist forces poison the water supply of the city of Acre (now a part of present day Israel) with typhoid bacteria, leading to a typhoid epidemic; another attempt is made to poison wells in Gaza with typhoid and dysentery.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Morris and Kedar 2023

title: Native Africans resist removal from land due to impending filling of Kariba Dam in the Zambezi watershed
description: The African people living in the Zambezi River Valley protest and resist removal from their home land, even as British colonizers fill the newly built Kariba Dam and threaten to prosecute demonstrators and burn homes and crops. During at least one protest that turned violent, eight Tonga people are shot and killed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Serpell 2020

title: Burmese government forces recapture Gyobyu Waterworks, previously occupied by rebel forces
description: Burma government forces recapture the Gyobyu Waterworks in 1951, which had been occupied by rebel forces for three years.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; New York Times 1951

title: Israel and Syria fight over Yarmouk River
description: Jordan makes public its plans to irrigate the Jordan Valley by tapping the Yarmouk River; Israel responds by commencing drainage of the Huleh swamps located in the demilitarized zone between Israel and Syria; border skirmishes ensue between Israel and Syria.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Wolf 1997 ; Samson and Charrier 1997

title: North Korea floods Pukhan Valley
description: North Korea releases flood waves from the Hwachon Dam damaging floating bridges operated by UN troops in the Pukhan Valley. The US Navy then sends planes to destroy the spillway crest gates.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; US Army Corps of Engineers 1953

title: Syrian forces fire on Israeli workers draining Huleh swamps
description: Syrian forces open fire on Israeli workers engaged in draining the Huleh Swamp, in northeastern Israel in 1951, wounding one. The Syrian Government argues that the reclamation work violates the Israel-Syrian armistice agreement.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Telegraphic Agency 1951 ; U.S. Department of State 1951

title: US Bombers Destroy Korea's Hwacheon Dam
description: The Hwacheon Dam in Korea, completed in 1944, becomes both a target and a tool of opposing forces during the Korean War. In 1951, North Korea opens the dam to flood downstream areas and slow advancing UN forces. In response, the US Navy sends aircraft to bomb the dam, the last known American use of aerial torpedoes in war.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Calcagno 2004

title: A water pipeline is cut and the repair party attacked in Malaya during the extended communist insurgency
description: During the communist insurgency in Malaya between 1948 and 1960, civilian water infrastructure was attacked. In 1952 in Tanjong Malim a water pipeline is cut and the party repairing it was ambushed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Short 1975

title: UN Command air forces conduct a series of massive bombings of 13 North Korean hydroelectric facilities
description: In June 1952, UN Command forces bomb a series of hydroelectric dams in North Korea on the Yalu River, including the Sui-ho dam, Kyosen dam, Fusen dam and Choisen dam. The attacks temporarily knock out 90% of North Korea's power-production capacity. Follow up attacks continue through September 1952.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Futrell 1983

title: Additional attacks on Sui-ho dam conducted during the Korean War
description: A final attack of the Korean War on the Sui-ho hydroelectric facility by UN forces is conducted on June 7, 1953.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Futrell 1983

title: Israel and Syria clash over Sea of Galilee and the construction of the Israeli National Water Carrier
description: Israel begins construction of its National Water Carrier to transfer water from the north of the Sea of Galilee out of the Jordan basin to the Negev Desert for irrigation. Syrian military actions along the border and international disapproval lead Israel to move its intake to the Sea of Galilee.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Naff and Matson 1984 ; Samson and Charrier 1997

title: Massive additional attacks on North Korean dams are conducted during the Korean War
description: During May, 1953, the UN Command air units again bomb Sui-ho dam generators, and also bombs Toksan, Chasan, Kuwonga, Namsi, and Taechon dams. The ensuing floods destroy thousands of homes and threaten several million North Koreans with starvation.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Futrell 1983 ; Crane 2000 ; Cumings 2011

title: North Korean dam at Sui-ho attacked again by UN Command air forces during the Korean War
description: A new bombing attack on Sui-ho dam generators is conducted by UN Command air units in February 1953.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Futrell 1983

title: Mekong Committee Established
description: Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and South Vietnam establish the Committee for Coordination of Investigations of the Lower Mekong Basin (Mekong Committee) under UN auspices, the first institutional framework for Mekong cooperation.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; UN ECAFE (1957). Committee for Coordination of Investigations of the Lower Mekong Basin.

title: Syria clashes with Israeli forces in July/August 1957 dispute over Israeli water systems
description: In July and August 1957, Syria clashes with Israel in Lake Huleh area in dispute over completion of Israeli water and drainage works
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Telegraphic Agency 1957a

title: Syria clashes with Israeli forces in dispute over Israeli water systems, April 1957
description: In April 1957, Syria clashes with Israel in Lake Huleh area in dispute over completion of Israeli water and drainage works.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Telegraphic Agency 1957a

title: Syria kills Israeli engineer working on Huleh swamp water diversions
description: Syria kills an Israeli engineer from across the Jordan River while working in the Huleh Swamp area on water diversions.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Telegraphic Agency 1957b

title: Two guards of the Israeli water company, Mekorot, are killed
description: Two guards of the Israeli Mekorot water company are killed in Kibbutz Beit Govrin in August 1957.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Virtual Library 2024

title: A third set of clashes between India and Pakistan over Surma River control occurs in August 1958
description: In August 1958 a third round of clashes occur between India and Pakistan on the East Pakistan-Assam border in a conflict over ownership of fertile land along the Surma River, and a dispute over claims over control of the river.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Razvi 1971 ; New York Times 1958a

title: Egypt and Sudan clash over Nile
description: Egypt sends an unsuccessful military expedition into disputed territory amidst pending negotiations over the Nile waters, Sudanese general elections, and an Egyptian vote on Sudan-Egypt unification; Nile Water Treaty signed when pro-Egyptian government elected in Sudan.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Wolf 1997

title: India and Pakistan fight over Surma River control and land disputes
description: In March 1958 violent clashes begin between India and Pakistan on the East Pakistan-Assam border in a conflict over ownership of fertile land along the Surma River, and a dispute over claims over control of the river. A demand from Assam that Pakistan abandon claims over any portion of the Surma were considered by Pakistan to be military provocation.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Razvi 1971 ; New York Times 1958a

title: India and Pakistan fight over Surma River control and land disputes in a second round of clashes in May 1958
description: In May 1958 clashes reoccur between India and Pakistan on the East Pakistan-Assam border in a conflict over the Surma River, and a dispute over claims over control of the river.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Razvi 1971 ; New York Times 1958a

title: Israel and Syria clash over water diversions from Huleh swamp area
description: In November and December 1958, clashes restart between Israel and Syria over irrigation, farmland, and water diversions in the Huleh Swamp area, with intervention by UN peacekeepers.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; New York Times 1958c

title: Syria clashes with Israel over Huleh canal project
description: Over a series of days in late March 1958, Syria clashes with Israel in Lake Huleh area over Israel's work to dig a canal to drain water from the marshes.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Herald 1958: New York Times 1958b

title: Egypt-Sudan Nile Waters Agreement
description: Egypt and Sudan sign a comprehensive water-sharing agreement allocating 55.5 BCM annually to Egypt and 18.5 BCM to Sudan, enabling construction of the Aswan High Dam. Upstream states were excluded from negotiations.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; United Nations Treaty Series No. 6519; Gleick, P.H. (1993).

title: Indus Waters Treaty Signed
description: India and Pakistan, with World Bank mediation, sign the Indus Waters Treaty in Karachi. The treaty allocates the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India and the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan, resolving a decade of post-partition disputes.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; World Bank (1960). Indus Waters Treaty; Gleick, P.H. (1993). International Security 18(1).

title: Lake Chad Basin Commission Established
description: Cameroon, Chad, Niger, and Nigeria establish the Lake Chad Basin Commission (LCBC) in Fort-Lamy to coordinate development and management of Lake Chad and its basin, one of Africa's earliest multilateral water bodies.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Convention and Statute Relating to the Development of the Chad Basin, Fort Lamy (1964); LCBC Secretariat.

title: US bombs irrigation systems in Vietnam
description: Irrigation water supply systems in North Vietnam are bombed during the Vietnam War. An estimated 661 sections of dikes damaged or destroyed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Kandachi 1967 ; Gleick 1993 ; Zemmali 1995

title: Violent dispute over access to irrigation water in the Al-Chibayish marshes of Iraq during drought
description: Disputes in the Al-Chibayish Marshes, part of Dhi Qar and Basrah governorates, escalate to armed fighting between two clans in the 1960s. One report describes a bloody dispute between the two clans over the allocation of irrigation water for rice farms during droughts.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Al Hasan 2020

title: Columbia River Treaty Signed
description: The United States and Canada sign the Columbia River Treaty, providing for construction of three dams in British Columbia for flood control and hydropower. The US secures flood control and pays Canada nearly $65 million; Canada receives half the downstream power benefits.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Treaty Between Canada and the United States of America Relating to Cooperative Development (1961).

title: Brazil and Paraguay clash over Paraná River
description: Negotiations between Brazil and Paraguay over the development of the Paraná River are interrupted by a unilateral show of military force by Brazil in 1962, which invades the area and claims control over the Guadalajara Falls site. Military forces are withdrawn in 1967 following an agreement for a joint commission to examine development in the region.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Murphy and Sabadell 1986

title: Israel destroys irrigation ditches in demilitarized zone on Syrian border
description: Israel destroys irrigation ditches in the lower Tarfiq in the demilitarized zone. Syria complains.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Naff and Matson 1984

title: Kaptai Dam displaces Jumma people in Eastern Pakistan
description: In 1957, Eastern Pakistan (present-day Bangladesh) begins building the Kaptai Hydroelectric Dam on the Karnaphuli River in the Chittagong Hills Tract in the southeast. Completed in 1962, the dam flooded 655 square kilometers of land and displaced 100,000 people, most of them Jumma, or ethnic minorities in a country ruled by a Bengali majority. The displaced Jumma are offered little land or compensation and many flee to neighboring India. These conditions contributed to 20+ years of conflict.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Chittagong Hill Tracts Commission 1991

title: A bomb is used to attack a Welsh dam to protest the flooding of a village
description: In February 1963, a bomb is used by the Mudiad Amddiffyn Cymru (Movement for the Defence of Wales) to attack an electricity transformer at a dam about to flood the village of Capel Celyn, Wales.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Laville 2023

title: Ethiopia and Somali nomads fight for desert water
description: Creation of boundaries in 1948 leaves Somali nomads under Ethiopian rule; border skirmishes occur over disputed territory in Ogaden desert where critical water and oil resources are located; cease-fire is negotiated only after several hundred are killed.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Wolf 1997

title: Niger Basin Act of Niamey
description: Nine Niger Basin states sign the Act of Niamey, committing to equitable navigation and economic cooperation over the Niger River, laying the groundwork for the later Niger River Commission and Niger Basin Authority.
countries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Mali, Niger, Nigeria
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Act regarding navigation and economic cooperation between the states of the Niger basin, Niamey (1963).

title: Cuba cuts off water to US at Guantanamo
description: On February 6, 1964, the Cuban government cuts off the normal water supply to the US Naval Base at Guantanamo Bay, in retaliation for the US seizure of four Cuban fishing boats days earlier near Florida.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Guantanamo Bay Gazette 1964

title: Israel drops bombs in a dispute over the source of the Dan River
description: Headwaters of the Dan River on the Jordan River are bombed at Tell El-Qadi in a dispute about sovereignty over the source of the Dan.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Naff and Matson 1984

title: River Niger Commission Founded
description: Ten riparian states establish the River Niger Commission at Niamey to promote joint studies and coordinate development of Niger Basin resources, entering into force in 1966.
countries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Chad
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Agreement concerning the River Niger Commission and the navigation and transport on the River Niger (1964).

title: Brazil and Paraguay military have a confrontation over the Paraná River
description: On June 17, 1965 Brazil sends a military detachment to occupy land along the Paraná River in order to make a claim on disputed borders between Brazil and Paraguay. This presence of Brazil’s military is considered a major "act of aggresion" and a violation of their territorial sovereignty.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Blanc 2018

title: British defend South African dam against possible saboteurs
description: President Kenneth Kaunda of Zambia calls on British government to send troops to Kariba Dam to protect it from possible saboteurs from Rhodesian government.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Chenje 2001

title: Feud over the Buffalo National River turns violent between environmentalists and local populations
description: Feuding between two groups over the fate of the Buffalo National River in Arkansas and a potential dam project turn violent when a canoe race on Memorial Day, 1965 is disrupted by barbed wire strung across the river and gun shots near the canoes. Small injuries caused by the barbed wire to canoeists are reported.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Schulte 2019

title: In a continuation of the dispute between Brazil and Paraguay over the Paraná River, a Brazilian military detachment makes arrest
description: Paraguay sends a military and diplomatic group to contested land on the border with Brazil. A Brazilian military detachment arrests them in a confrontation. This dispute precedes the construction of the major Itaipu Dam on the Paraná River.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Blanc 2018

title: Israel attacks over an Arab plan to divert headwaters of the Jordan River away from Israel
description: Fire is exchanged over "all-Arab" plan to divert the Jordan River headwaters (Hasbani and Banias) and presumably preempt Israeli National Water Carrier; Syria halts construction of its diversion in July 1966.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Wolf 1995 ; Wolf 1997

title: Palestinians attack Israeli water pumps for the National Water Carrier
description: First attack ever by the Palestinian National Liberation Movement Al-Fatah is on the diversion pumps for the Israeli National Water Carrier. Attack fails.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Naff and Matson 1984 ; Dolatyar 1995

title: Violent protest in Paraguay over Brazilian occupation of land along the Paraná River and control of the river
description: In a growing dispute over the control of the Paraná River between Paraguay and Brazil, Paraguayan protestors burn a Brazilian flag near the Brazilian embassy, and throw Molotov cocktails into Brazilian-owned businesses chanting ‘Paraguay sí. Bandeirantes no. Fuera los mamelucos’ (‘Paraguay yes, invaders no:out with the bastards’). Police disperse the crowd violently and arrest 15.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Blanc 2018

title: Israel attacks Jordan water works on the Banias
description: Israel destroys the Arab diversion works on the Jordan River headwaters. During Arab-Israeli War Israel occupies Golan Heights, with Banias tributary to the Jordan; Israel occupies West Bank.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Gleick 1993 ; Wolf 1995 ; Wolf 1997 ; Wallenstein and Swain 1997

title: Kuwait and Iraq fight over border dispute, destroying water wells
description: Kuwait and Iraq move troops to their frontier and recall their ambassadors after Iraqi border guards cross the frontier, destroy a tent camp of workers drilling water wells, and briefly occupy the area, according to reports from both countries.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; New York Times 1967

title: Palestinians attack civilian targets in Israel, destroying water pumps and irrigation equipment
description: In the spring of 1967, Palestinian groups attack civilian targets in Israel, including destroying water pumps and irrigation equipment in the north of the country.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Seliktar 2005

title: US attempts to flood land to slow Vietnamese military efforts
description: The US military, in 'Operation Popeye,' uses silver iodide for cloud seeding over Indochina (Vietnam), in an attempt to extend the monsoon season and stop the flow of materiel along Ho Chi Minh trail. "Continuous rainfall was intended to slow down the truck traffic and was relatively successful."
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Plant 1995 ; Troung and Cooper 2003

title: Youth International Party threatens to spike Chicago's water supply with LSD ahead of Democratic National Convention
description: The Youth International Party in the United States threatens to spike Lake Michigan with the hallucinogenic LSD. Lake Michigan serves as the city of Chicago's drinking water supply. The threat is targeted at the Democratic National Convention of 1968. No known poisonings occur.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Mohtadi and Murshid 2006 ; CBC News Online 2004

title: China and Soviet Union fight over navigation and control of the Amur River as part of disputes over shared waterways
description: An armed conflict between China and the Soviet Union breaks out over navigation and control of the Amur River in July 1969, part of an ongoing series of disputes over shared waterways.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; New York Times 1969

title: Egyptian commandos destroy water pipeline in Sinai desert north of Ismalia
description: Egypt claims to carry out four sabotage forays against Israeli positions in the Sinai Desert. Among other objectives, the commandos said they destroyed observation posts and blew up a water pipeline 10 miles north of Ismalia.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Jewish Telegraphic Agency 1969

title: Israel attacks East Ghor Canal, August 1969
description: On August 10, 1969 Israel again attacks the East Ghor Canal on the eastern bank of the Jordan River in reprisal for the shelling of Israeli border settlement and to pressure Jordan to stop Palestinian attacks in Israel from Jordanian territory.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Schmidt 1970

title: Israel attacks East Ghor Canal, June 1969
description: On June 5, 1969, Israel attacks the East Ghor Canal on the eastern bank of the Jordan River in reprisal for the shelling of Israeli border settlement and in an effort to pressure Jordan to prevent Palestinian attacks in Israel from Jordanian territory.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Schmidt 1970

title: Palestinian group attempts to pollute Israeli water with attack on an oil pipeline
description: The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) places an explosive device on the Trans-Arabian Pipeline in Jordan in an attempt to pollute water that provides drinking water and water for fisheries to Israel in the Hutch Valley. While the explosive device did cause significant damage to the pipeline, reports do not indicate that water supplies were affected.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; RAND Database of Worldwide Terrorism Incidents 2018 ; Heradstveit 2017

title: There are multiple attacks on Belfast's water supply system, Northern Ireland
description: Four separate explosions occur in April, 1969, damaging water-supply infrastructure in Northern Ireland. The first explosion occurs at a water installation serving Belfast at Dunadry, County Antrim. The second occurs at Silent Valley reservoir in County Down and temporarily interrupts water supply for Belfast. The third occurs a few days later at a water pipeline between Lugh Neagh and Belfast. The fourth occurs near a water pipeline, disrupting water to Belfast for several days. The explosions are first blamed on the Irish Republican Army (IRA), but are later connected to the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and the Ulster Protestant Volunteers (UPV).
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Melaugh 2019

title: Alleged plot to contaminate US water supply
description: The Weathermen, a group opposed to American imperialism and the Vietnam War, allegedly attempts to obtain biological agents to contaminate the water supply systems of US urban centers.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Kupperman and Trent 1979 ; Eitzen and Takafuji 1997 ; Purver 1995

title: Aswan High Dam Completed
description: Egypt completes the Aswan High Dam, creating Lake Nasser (the world's largest man-made lake). Sudan agrees to resettle 100,000 Nubian residents displaced by the reservoir, and Egypt compensates Sudan for flooded territory.
source: Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology; Biswas, A.K. (2002). Aswan High Dam: An Environmental and Socio-Economic Assessment. International Journal of Water Resources Development.

title: Israel attacks East Ghor Canal, January 1970
